source.title: PowerShell 7
source.versionPolicy: The supported PowerShell 7 LTS channel is the baseline; differences in newer stable releases are recorded per document.

notes: The shell manual is original project text synthesized from the listed official topics rather than a copy of one upstream page.
Launcher and selected language behavior were checked with PowerShell 7.6.3 on Linux and PowerShell 7.6.4 on Windows; macOS and remaining platform-specific behavior remain outstanding.
This document is the navigation index; pwsh7.md is the primary shell and language manual.
Alias availability must be checked at runtime for each targeted release and platform.
The navigation index introduces no separate runtime behavior; evidence and remaining platform boundaries belong to the linked pages.
The page is an original task-oriented adaptation of the launcher reference.
Launcher help and selected exit behavior were checked with PowerShell 7.6.3 on Linux and PowerShell 7.6.4 on Windows; macOS and remaining platform-specific behavior remain outstanding.
The page distinguishes cross-platform parsing from the Windows-only stop-parsing token.

PowerShell 7.6.3 Linux and 7.6.4 Windows smoke evidence covers the parsing examples; macOS remains pending. Windows catalog harnesses demonstrated two whitespace failures: variable/parameter merging can fail a read before plausible downstream null/default counts, while Where-Object document-eq$name remains syntactically valid but silently selects zero rows. The shared guidance now requires explicit predicates, fail-fast reads, and expected coverage invariants.
The page is original guidance emphasizing literal data and native-command boundaries.

PowerShell 7.6.4 on Windows confirmed indexed interpolation versus subexpression selection, invariant interpolation versus de-DE ToString conversion with culture restoration, and literal child source; Linux parser evidence also covers the page. macOS, here-string and smart-quote edges, Unicode, and target-native parsers remain outstanding.
The page treats cmdlet object pipelines and native-command boundaries separately.

PowerShell 7.6.4 on Windows confirmed the documented native-byte boundary, bounded Export-Csv no-clobber fixture, and the fact that uncaptured .NET/cmdlet success results contaminate enclosing output unless precisely captured or suppressed; macOS and remaining Linux platform behavior remain outstanding.

PowerShell 7.6.4 parser evidence on 2026-08-12 confirmed that a bare foreach statement before a pipe raises EmptyPipeElement, while array/subexpression wrapping and an invoked script block each pass the two emitted objects to Measure-Object.

A ManT-result audit falsely counted one diagnostic because an omitted optional property produced null and @($null) is a one-element array. PowerShell 7.6.4 confirmed wrapped=1, direct null Count=0, and a property/value-gated count=0; the page now makes this Agent evidence boundary searchable.

Runtime metadata and the official New-Item reference confirm Path exists but LiteralPath does not. The corrected output-suppression example uses -Path and requires target validation; the smoke suite locks this distinction.
The page separates stream routing from error and native exit-status policy.
PowerShell 7.6.4 on Windows confirmed the documented native-byte boundary and overwrite behavior; macOS and remaining Linux platform behavior remain outstanding.

A 2026-08-12 isolated cmd.exe probe wrote one stderr line and returned 7. With ErrorActionPreference Stop, 2>&1, and PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference false, PowerShell 7.6.4 completed the assignment with one ErrorRecord and preserved LASTEXITCODE 7; no file or system state changed.
The page indexes all 47 automatic-variable headings in the locked PowerShell 7.6 source and distinguishes PowerShell success state from native process exit status.

PowerShell 7.6.4 on Windows confirmed the stable platform and language-context examples. In an ordinary non-debugger session, ConsoleFileName and PSDebugContext were absent rather than present with null values; macOS, Linux, debugger, event, remoting, and legacy console-file contexts remain outstanding.
The page is original guidance emphasizing reproducible automation and profile safety.

PowerShell 7.6.4 in a clean Windows NoProfile process confirmed that PROFILE is a string equal to CurrentUserCurrentHost and exposes all four documented profile-path properties. No profile file was read or created; loading order, host behavior, policy, remoting, macOS, Linux, and other configurations remain outstanding.
The page is original guidance emphasizing stable parameter contracts and streaming pipeline input.

PowerShell 7.6.4 on Windows confirmed advanced-function begin/process/end timing and that an unsuppressed collection Add return value contaminates normal output. The in-memory language behavior remains to be repeated on macOS and Linux.
This is an original guide, not an official about-topic name; its upstream source covers native-command parsing behavior.

PowerShell 7.6.4 on Windows confirmed native resolution, Windows argument mode, exit and merged-error boundaries, BOM-less UTF-8, and exact redirected bytes; Linux 7.6.3 covered selected native resolution and exit behavior. macOS, remaining Linux encoding cases, stdin, target parsers, and arbitrary tools remain outstanding.
The page emphasizes command precedence and source discovery in cross-platform sessions.

PowerShell 7.6.4 in a clean Windows NoProfile process confirmed alias precedence over a same-name function, ordered All results, and a nonempty Syntax view. The suite also checks core command, Windows alias, native-name, and documented-option metadata; module, provider, PATH, macOS, and Linux variance remains outstanding.

The dual-edition NoProfile provider fixture passes 14/14: fixed built-in paths return the documented provider object types; FileSystem, Registry, and Certificate expose different dynamic parameters; Get-Help -Path Cert:\ returns provider-customized help; and Get-PSDrive can change later provider discovery by loading Microsoft.PowerShell.Security. It emits no environment value, registry data, certificate, or user path and performs no provider mutation or network access.
The page distinguishes installed help, online help, and downloadable help content.

PowerShell 7.6.4 in a clean Windows NoProfile process confirmed named parameter help and syntax fallback for an in-memory function without detailed help. The probe performed no update, GUI, network, or profile-content operation; provider, downloadable, GUI, macOS, and Linux help remains outstanding.

The dual-edition NoProfile provider fixture passes 14/14: fixed built-in paths return the documented provider object types; FileSystem, Registry, and Certificate expose different dynamic parameters; Get-Help -Path Cert:\ returns provider-customized help; and Get-PSDrive can change later provider discovery by loading Microsoft.PowerShell.Security. It emits no environment value, registry data, certificate, or user path and performs no provider mutation or network access.
The page emphasizes object inspection before formatting or property access.

PowerShell 7.6.4 on Windows confirmed an in-memory custom object exposes Name and Count before formatting, while Format-Table output exposes formatting-system records instead. Platform/provider-specific types remain outstanding.
The page emphasizes pure filtering predicates and source-side filtering when available.

PowerShell 7.6.4 on Windows confirmed -InputObject evaluates a three-item array once while pipeline input evaluates its three members and selects the two enabled objects. Provider-specific filtering and macOS/Linux repetition remain outstanding.
The page distinguishes streaming use from side-effectful actions and parallel execution.

PowerShell 7.6.4 on Windows confirmed one -InputObject invocation versus three pipeline invocations, begin/item/end phase order, and that a bounded -Parallel probe returned every input without ordinary caller-variable visibility. macOS/Linux and action-specific concurrency remain outstanding.
The page emphasizes preserving object shape before formatting or serialization and documents the distinct First/Last/Skip versus SkipLast parameter sets.

PowerShell 7.6.4 on Windows confirmed complete parameter metadata, First+Last+Skip selection, the incompatible SkipLast combination, unique-value case policy, and parse-valid examples. Provider objects, resource limits, macOS, Linux, and calculated-property variants remain outstanding.
The page emphasizes provider boundaries, literal paths, bounded enumeration, source-side FileSystem Filter semantics, and PowerShell-side Include/Exclude semantics.

PowerShell 7.6.4 on Windows confirmed complete parameter metadata, parse-valid examples, and a bounded SystemRoot FileSystemInfo result. Provider, path, symlink, mount, permission, macOS, and Linux behavior remains outstanding.

The dual-edition NoProfile provider fixture passes 14/14: fixed built-in paths return the documented provider object types; FileSystem, Registry, and Certificate expose different dynamic parameters; Get-Help -Path Cert:\ returns provider-customized help; and Get-PSDrive can change later provider discovery by loading Microsoft.PowerShell.Security. It emits no environment value, registry data, certificate, or user path and performs no provider mutation or network access.
The page emphasizes bounded, reproducible sort contracts.
PowerShell 7.6.4 on Windows confirmed Stable/Top/Bottom metadata and stable equal-key order b,a,c on in-memory objects. Culture/provider cases and macOS/Linux repetition remain outstanding.
The page emphasizes command conflicts, trusted sources, and reproducible module selection.

PowerShell 7.6.4 on Windows imported only a trusted GUID-temporary fixture: -NoClobber retained an existing function, -Prefix Probe created the prefixed command, and -PassThru returned the fixture module. It was unloaded and removed; third-party, binary, remote, macOS and Linux compatibility remain outstanding.
The page explicitly warns against downloading remote content into Invoke-Expression.
PowerShell 7.6.3 on Linux and PowerShell 7.6.4 on Windows confirmed that irm resolves to Invoke-RestMethod; macOS remains outstanding.
The page adds explicit artifact-verification guidance for downloads.
PowerShell 7.6.3 on Linux and PowerShell 7.6.4 on Windows confirmed that iwr resolves to Invoke-WebRequest; macOS remains outstanding.
The page treats parsing data as code as a security risk, documents safer alternatives, and explains that -Command binds pipeline strings by value and evaluates each item separately.
PowerShell 7.6.3 on Linux and PowerShell 7.6.4 on Windows confirmed that iex resolves to Invoke-Expression; macOS remains outstanding.
Runtime verification on the PowerShell 7.6 Linux authoring environment found no built-in irx command.
The page is an availability guide for a custom shorthand, not a claim about a universal alias mapping.
The page is a platform-specific command-resolution guide rather than a claim that curl is a universal built-in alias.
PowerShell 7.6.4 on Windows and PowerShell 7.6.3 on Linux confirmed native curl resolution without a built-in curl alias; macOS and environment-specific executable availability remain outstanding.

The guide emphasizes when direct native invocation is preferable and explains wait, exit-code, stream, and argument-list pitfalls. Microsoft's .NET Process contract supplies the dual-redirected-stream deadlock boundary.

Core behavior was checked with PowerShell 7.6.3 on Linux; PowerShell 7.6.4 on Windows confirmed complete parameter metadata and the bounded smoke examples. A Windows PowerShell 5.1 harness reproduced the shared .NET sequential-read deadlock pattern and concurrent reads avoided it; macOS and remaining platform-specific behavior remain outstanding.

PowerShell 7 runtime metadata confirmed ProcessStartInfo exposes both Arguments and the structured ArgumentList collection. The page distinguishes the .NET property from the Start-Process -ArgumentList parameter and warns that shared Windows PowerShell 5.1 code cannot assume the property exists.
The page distinguishes the Windows-only PowerShell alias from the cmd.exe start builtin and records its absence on non-Windows PowerShell 7.
PowerShell 7.6.3 on Linux confirmed that the start alias is absent by default.
The guide highlights exact-path input, provider-dependent actions, pipeline binding, and the risk of opening untrusted items.

PowerShell 7.6.4 on Windows confirmed the ii alias and every documented option against live metadata; Linux 7.6.3 confirmed the alias. No item or GUI handler was invoked; provider actions, associations, desktop behavior, policy, and macOS remain outstanding.
The page documents the common ii . workflow while preserving the broader provider semantics and trust boundary.
PowerShell 7.6.3 on Linux confirmed that ii resolves to Invoke-Item.
The guide treats PowerShell 7 and Windows PowerShell 5.1 as separately verified runtimes.

Separate Windows PowerShell 5.1.26100.8875 and PowerShell 7.6.4 suites confirm edition, version-table keys, command resolution, encoding, question-mark wrappers, and parameter differences. Module, .NET, remoting, provider, application, macOS, and Linux migration workloads remain outstanding.
